summary: Specifies the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, a framework for passing configuration information to hosts. Based on BOOTP, it adds automatic allocation of reusable network addresses and extra configuration options. It was replaced by RFC 2131.

plainLanguage.summary: When you arrive at a hotel, the front desk gives you a room key and tells you the rules. DHCP gives a new computer its network settings.

questions: what are dhcp discover offer request ack
what are dhcp t1 and t2 timers
subtitle: How a host on a TCP/IP network gets an IP address and other settings automatically from a server, on a lease.

tldr.problem: Hosts need many configuration values, above all an IP address, and typing them in by hand on every host is error-prone and does not let scarce addresses be reused.
tldr.mechanism: A client broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER, servers answer with DHCPOFFER, the client picks one with DHCPREQUEST, and the chosen server commits the lease and replies with DHCPACK. The format reuses BOOTP, so relay agents and BOOTP clients keep working.
tldr.outcome: Addresses can be handed out for a limited time and reclaimed. This document was reissued from RFC 1531 and was itself replaced by RFC 2131.

today: RFC 1541 is obsolete: it was replaced by RFC 2131. It was itself a reissue of RFC 1531, which it obsoleted to fix errors introduced in editing, and it was a Proposed Standard.

sections.title: What DHCP Provides
sections.content:
The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) delivers configuration parameters to Internet hosts. It has two parts: a protocol for carrying host-specific parameters from a DHCP server to a DHCP client, and a mechanism for allocating network addresses to hosts.

DHCP supports three kinds of IP address allocation. In automatic allocation a host gets a permanent address. In dynamic allocation it gets an address for a limited period, or until it gives the address up. In manual allocation the administrator picks the address and DHCP only conveys it. Only dynamic allocation lets an address be reused automatically.

The design goals include no manual configuration of hosts, no server needed on every subnet, coexistence with statically configured hosts, and service to existing BOOTP clients. DHCP does not register hosts with the DNS and is not intended for configuring routers. A host should not act as a DHCP server unless an administrator has configured it to.
sections.plainLanguage: The network can give you a permanent seat, a seat for a while, or a seat the manager picked. Only the 'for a while' seats can be given to someone else later.

sections.title: The DHCP Message and Its BOOTP Roots
sections.content:
DHCP uses the BOOTP message format from RFC 951, so existing BOOTP clients can talk to DHCP servers and BOOTP relay agents can pass DHCP messages along. The op field is BOOTREQUEST (1) from client to server and BOOTREPLY (2) from server to client. Fixed fields include xid (a transaction ID chosen by the client), ciaddr, yiaddr (the address given to the client), siaddr, giaddr (the relay agent), chaddr (the client hardware address), sname and file.

The BOOTP vendor extensions field is renamed the options field, now variable length with a 312-octet minimum. It starts with the four-octet magic cookie, the decimal values 99, 130, 83 and 99. The DHCP message type option must be in every message. A new client identifier option lets a client identify itself with something other than its hardware address. Messages travel over UDP: to port 67 for server-bound messages and to port 68 for client-bound ones.

The leftmost bit of the flags field is the BROADCAST flag. A client that cannot receive unicast IP datagrams before it has an address SHOULD set it to 1, which hints to servers and relay agents to broadcast replies.
sections.plainLanguage: A DHCP message is a form with fixed boxes to fill in, like name, address and ticket number, plus a blank area for extra notes. It reuses an older form so old machines can still read it.

sections.title: Getting and Reusing an Address
sections.content:
In the full exchange, the client broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER, optionally suggesting an address and lease time. Each server may reply with DHCPOFFER carrying an address in yiaddr. The client may collect several offers and chooses one by broadcasting DHCPREQUEST with the server identifier option naming the chosen server. That server commits the binding and replies DHCPACK. Servers that were not chosen treat the broadcast as a declined offer. If the server cannot satisfy the request, it SHOULD answer DHCPNAK.

Before using the address the client performs a final check, for example an ARP request. If the address looks to be in use, it sends DHCPDECLINE and restarts. A client that no longer needs its address may send DHCPRELEASE, though correct operation does not depend on it.

A client that remembers an address can skip ahead: it broadcasts a DHCPREQUEST with that address in ciaddr, and servers that know it answer DHCPACK, or DHCPNAK if the request is invalid, for example because the client moved subnets.
sections.plainLanguage: You shout 'is anyone there who can give me a seat?' Several people may offer one. You say 'I will take yours', and they write it down and say 'confirmed'.

sections.title: Leases, Timers and Client States
sections.content:
A lease lasts a fixed period, measured in seconds. The value 0xffffffff means infinity and the minimum lease duration is one hour. Times are relative to the client's own clock, because client and server clocks may not be synchronized.

The client keeps two timers. At T1 it enters the RENEWING state and unicasts a DHCPREQUEST to the server that issued the address. At T2, if no DHCPACK has arrived, it enters REBINDING and broadcasts the request to any server. T1 defaults to 0.5 times the lease duration and T2 to 0.875 times, and both should have some random fuzz. If the lease expires before an acknowledgment arrives, the client MUST immediately stop network processing and go back to INIT. If it is given a new address, it MUST NOT keep using the old one.

Retransmission uses randomized exponential backoff. The first delay MUST be 4 seconds randomized by a value from -1 to +1, then 8 seconds, doubling up to a maximum of 64 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Your hotel stay has a checkout time. Halfway through you ask the front desk if you can stay longer. If they do not answer, you ask anyone at the hotel. If time runs out, you must leave the room.

sections.title: Server Behavior and Choosing Parameters
sections.content:
For a DHCPDISCOVER, the server picks an address in this order: the client's previous address if it is available, else the address in the Requested IP Address option if valid and free, else a new address from its pool. A server may, for administrative reasons, assign a different address or refuse a client. It is not required to answer every message, and the specification leaves administrative controls to implementations.

The server identifies a client by the client identifier option, or by chaddr if the option is absent. For lease time it returns the existing expiration for a client that already has an address and asks for nothing, a locally configured default for a new client that asks for nothing, or it may honor or change a requested lease. Offered parameters follow a strict order of rules, so that all servers give uniform answers. A DHCPDECLINE makes the server mark the address as not allocated and SHOULD alert the administrator. Appendix A lists the IP, link-layer and TCP parameters that DHCP can supply, taken from the Host Requirements RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: The desk first tries to give you the room you had before. If it is taken, it tries the one you asked for. If that is taken too, it gives you any free room.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states plainly that DHCP in its current form is quite insecure. It is built directly on UDP and IP, which are inherently insecure, and it is meant to ease maintenance of remote or diskless hosts that are hard to configure with passwords or keys.

Unauthorized DHCP servers can easily be set up and could send false, disruptive information to clients, such as incorrect or duplicate IP addresses, incorrect routing information or spoof nameserver addresses. Malicious clients could masquerade as legitimate ones to retrieve their information, or claim all dynamically allocated resources for themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can pretend to be the front desk and hand out wrong keys, and anyone can pretend to be a guest. The protocol has no way to check.

messages.label: DHCPDISCOVER
messages.note: Broadcast on the local subnet to find servers.

messages.label: DHCPOFFER
messages.note: Offers an address in yiaddr and other parameters.

messages.label: DHCPREQUEST
messages.note: Broadcast; names the chosen server in the server identifier option.

messages.label: DHCPACK
messages.note: Commits the binding and carries the configuration.

viz.caption: FORMAT OF A DHCP MESSAGE (RFC 1541, FIGURE 1)

fields.name: htype
fields.desc: Hardware address type, for example 1 for 10mb ethernet.

fields.name: hlen
fields.desc: Hardware address length, for example 6 for 10mb ethernet.

fields.name: hops
fields.desc: Client sets to zero; optionally used by relay agents.

fields.name: xid
fields.desc: Transaction ID chosen by the client.

fields.name: secs
fields.desc: Seconds elapsed since the client started trying to boot.

fields.name: flags
fields.desc: Leftmost bit is the BROADCAST flag; the rest must be zero.

fields.name: ciaddr
fields.desc: Client IP address, when verifying or renewing one.

fields.name: siaddr
fields.desc: Address of the next server to use in bootstrap.

fields.name: options
fields.desc: Options, 312 octets minimum, starting with the magic cookie.
